---
title: "Sensitivity analyses"
subtitle: "How the association between SHBG and skeletal muscle mass depends on each covariate, on the measure of body size, on the specification and on the sample"
metadata-files: [_report.yml]
---

```{r}
#| code-summary: "Code: setup, and checks that the statements of the text hold in the data"
source("_common.R")
sen <- tab("tableS_sensitivity")
other <- sapply(paste0("B", 2:8), function(k) pct(SE[[k]]$ratio))            # one covariate other than waist removed
spec  <- sapply(paste0("E", 1:4), function(k) pct(SE[[k]]$ratio))
samp  <- sapply(paste0("F", 1:5), function(k) pct(SE[[k]]$ratio))
NL <- rows(R$nonlinearity)
P <- function(k) SE[[k]]$p
# statements made in the text must hold in the data
stopifnot(P("A5") > 0.05, P("B1") < 0.001, all(sapply(paste0("B", 2:8), P) > 0.05), P("A3") < 0.001, P("A4") > 0.05,
          all(sapply(c("C1", "C2", "C4", "C5", "C6"), P) > 0.05), P("C3") < 0.001, P("C7") < 0.001,
          P("D1") > 0.05, P("D2") > 0.05, all(sapply(c(paste0("E", 1:4), "F2", "F3", "F4", "F5"), P) > 0.05), P("F1") < 0.05,
          NL$p_nonlinearity[1] > 0.05, NL$p_nonlinearity[2] < 0.001, NL$p_per_10[1] > 0.05)
```

All estimates are percent differences in mean skeletal muscle mass per doubling of SHBG. The models are defined
in [Model definition](models.html#sensitivity-models). The primary model was defined after an initial model had been
fitted, and the sensitivity analyses describe the robustness of a single association; they were not adjusted for
multiple testing.

## Role of each covariate and of the measure of body size

![(A) Adjusted mean skeletal muscle mass across SHBG in the primary model (solid line) and in the primary model without waist circumference (dashed line); bands are 95% confidence intervals. (B) Percent difference in mean skeletal muscle mass per doubling of SHBG when one covariate is removed from the primary model; the five hormone covariates were removed together. (C) The same difference when body size is measured in other ways: another measure in place of height or waist circumference, a further measure added to the primary model (+), or the covariates of the initial model. The filled point and the dotted line mark the primary model. Fig 2 of the manuscript.](`r fig("Fig2")`){width=88%}

- **Waist circumference is the only covariate that matters.** Without it the estimate is `r est(SE$B1)`. With any other
  covariate removed it stays between `r fmt(min(other), 2)`% and `r fmt(max(other), 2)`%.
- **The sequential models show the same step.** The estimate is `r est(SE$A3)` after adjustment for age, race/ethnicity
  and height, and `r est(SE$A4)` once waist circumference is added.
- **The result does not depend on waist circumference as the measure of body size.** With body mass index in place of
  height and waist circumference the estimate is `r est(SE$C1)`, and with weight in place of waist circumference
  `r est(SE$C2)`. It stays close to zero when percent body fat (`r fmt(pct(SE$C4$ratio), 2)`%), body mass index
  (`r fmt(pct(SE$C5$ratio), 2)`%) or fat mass (`r fmt(pct(SE$C6$ratio), 2)`%) is added to the primary model.
- **The exception is body composition from impedance as the only measure of adiposity.** With fat mass in place of
  waist circumference the estimate is `r est(SE$C3)`, and with the covariates of the initial model `r est(SE$C7)`.

### Why the impedance-based measures behave differently

Percent body fat is a proportion. It correlates weakly with absolute muscle mass (ρ = `r fmt(S$spearman_smm_pbf, 2)`)
and less strongly with SHBG (ρ = `r fmt(S$spearman_shbg_pbf, 2)`) than waist circumference does
(ρ = `r fmt(S$spearman_shbg_waist, 2)`), so it captures less of what the two variables share. In addition, percent body
fat and fat mass come from the same impedance measurement as skeletal muscle mass: the fat-free mass implied by weight
and percent body fat has a correlation of `r fmt(S$pearson_smm_ffm, 2)` with skeletal muscle mass. These variables are
partly determined by the outcome, which makes them poor measures of body size for this purpose.

## Scaling, specification and sample

![Percent difference in mean skeletal muscle mass per doubling of SHBG, with 95% confidence intervals, under sequential adjustment, alternative scaling of muscle mass, alternative specifications and restricted samples. The filled point and the dotted line mark the primary model.](`r fig("S4_Fig")`){width=88%}

- **Scaling of muscle mass.** As an index (kg/m², without height as a covariate) the estimate is `r est(SE$D1)`; as a
  percentage of body weight, `r est(SE$D2)`.
- **Specification.** Robust standard errors, a Gaussian model, a log-linear model and untransformed hormone covariates
  give estimates between `r fmt(min(spec), 2)`% and `r fmt(max(spec), 2)`%.
- **Sample.** Restrictions give estimates between `r fmt(min(samp), 2)`% and `r fmt(max(samp), 2)`%. The only confidence
  interval that excludes zero is the one obtained without the `r S$n_cook_excluded` observations with a Cook's distance
  above 4/n: `r est(SE$F1)`, `r ptext(SE$F1$p)`. A small association cannot be ruled out.

## All specifications

```{r}
kt(data.frame(ID = sen$id, Group = sub("^[A-G]\\. ", "", sen$group), Specification = ufix(sen$specification), n = fmt(sen$n, 0),
              `Ratio of means (95% CI)` = paste0(fmt(sen$ratio, 3), " (", ci(sen$lcl, sen$ucl, 3), ")"),
              `Difference, % (95% CI)` = paste0(fmt(sen$pct_difference, 2), " (", ci(pct(sen$lcl), pct(sen$ucl)), ")"),
              `P value` = pval(sen$p), check.names = FALSE), align = "lllrrrr")
```

Per doubling of SHBG. In D1 height is not a covariate. In C7 the covariates are those of the initial model.

## Shape of the association

```{r}
kt(data.frame(Model = NL$model, `Term tested` = NL$term_tested, `AIC, log2(SHBG)` = fmt(NL$aic_log2, 1), `AIC, SHBG linear` = fmt(NL$aic_linear, 1),
              `AIC, spline (3 df)` = fmt(NL$aic_spline_3df, 1),
              `Test against the spline` = paste0("F = ", fmt(NL$F_nonlinearity, 2), " (df = ", NL$df1, " and ", fmt(NL$df2, 0), "); ", ptext(NL$p_nonlinearity)),
              `Ratio per 10 nmol/L, SHBG linear (95% CI)` = paste0(fmt(NL$ratio_per_10, 3), " (", ci(NL$lcl_per_10, NL$ucl_per_10, 3), ")"),
              check.names = FALSE), align = "llrrrlr")
```

In the primary model there is no evidence of departure from linearity on the logarithmic scale, and SHBG entered as an
untransformed linear term leads to the same conclusion (`r ptext(NL$p_per_10[1])`). With the covariates of the initial
model a linear term does not describe the association: the slope is steeper at low concentrations and flattens at
high ones, and the logarithm fits better. This is one of the reasons for the logarithmic scale of the primary model.

![Ratio of mean skeletal muscle mass relative to the median SHBG. (A) Primary model: the term for log2(SHBG) and a natural cubic spline of log2(SHBG). (B) Initial model: the linear term for SHBG and a natural cubic spline of SHBG.](`r fig("S3_Fig")`){width=90%}

## Initial model

```{r}
ti <- tab("tableS_submitted_model")
kt(data.frame(Variable = term_label(ti$term, ti$label),
              `Ratio of means (95% CI)` = paste0(fmt(ti$ratio, 3), " (", ci(ti$lcl, ti$ucl, 3), ")"),
              `Difference in mean, %` = fmt(ti$pct_difference, 2), `P value` = pval(ti$p), check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrr")
```

The model specified first, with SHBG and the hormones on their original scale and percent body fat as the only measure
of body composition ([definition and reasons for its revision](models.html#initial-model-and-reasons-for-its-revision)).
It gives `r fmt(pct(SUB$terms$shbg$ratio), 2)`% per 10 nmol/L of SHBG
(95% CI `r ci(pct(SUB$terms$shbg$lcl), pct(SUB$terms$shbg$ucl))`). One participant had a testosterone concentration of
`r fmt(SUB$max_testosterone_ng_dl, 0)` ng/dL (`r fmt(SUB$max_testosterone_nmol_l, 1)` nmol/L), with a leverage of
`r fmt(SUB$max_leverage, 2)` and a Cook's distance of `r fmt(SUB$max_cook, 1)` in this model. In the primary model, in
which the hormones are on the logarithmic scale, excluding her gives `r est(SE$F5)`.

## SHBG as the dependent variable

```{r}
so <- tab("tableS_shbg_outcome")
lab_of <- function(d) { l <- c(tab("table2_primary_model")$label, ti$label); names(l) <- c(tab("table2_primary_model")$term, ti$term); unname(l[d$term]) }
show_so <- function(m) { d <- so[so$model == m, ]
  kt(data.frame(Variable = term_label(d$term, lab_of(d)), `Ratio of mean SHBG (95% CI)` = paste0(fmt(d$ratio, 3), " (", ci(d$lcl, d$ucl, 3), ")"),
                `P value` = pval(d$p), check.names = FALSE), align = "lrr") }
sp <- R$shbg_outcome$primary
sjt <- rows(R$shbg_outcome$joint)
sjf <- function(term) paste0("F = ", fmt(sjt$F[sjt$term == term], 2), " (df = ", sjt$df[sjt$term == term], " and ", fmt(sjt$df_residual[1], 0), "; ", ptext(sjt$p[sjt$term == term]), ")")
stopifnot(sp$smm$p > 0.05, sp$waist_cm$p < 0.001, R$shbg_outcome$submitted_smm$p < 0.001,
          sp[["log2(estradiol)"]]$p < 0.001, sp[["log2(estradiol)"]]$ratio > 1, sp[["log2(dheas)"]]$p < 0.001, sp[["log2(dheas)"]]$ratio < 1,
          sjt$p[sjt$term == "race"] < 0.001, sjt$p[sjt$term == "status"] < 0.05)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Covariates of the primary model (Table 3 of the manuscript)

```{r}
show_so("Covariates of the primary model")
```

Joint $F$ tests: race/ethnicity, `r sjf("race")`; menopausal status, `r sjf("status")`; activity limitation,
`r sjf("activity_limit")`. The model explains `r fmt(100 * R$shbg_outcome$deviance_explained, 1)`% of the deviance.

## Covariates of the initial model

```{r}
show_so("Covariates of the initial model")
```

:::

Complementary gamma log-link model with SHBG as the dependent variable. The concentration of SHBG responds to
adiposity and to other hormones, so it is natural to read the association with SHBG as the variable to be explained.
Read in that direction the conclusion is the same. With the covariates of the primary model, skeletal muscle mass is
not associated with SHBG (ratio per kilogram `r fmt(sp$smm$ratio, 3)`; 95% CI `r ci(sp$smm$lcl, sp$smm$ucl, 3)`), whereas
mean SHBG is `r fmt(abs(pct(sp$waist_cm$ratio)), 1)`% lower for each 5 cm of waist circumference,
`r fmt(pct(sp[["log2(estradiol)"]]$ratio), 1)`% higher for each doubling of estradiol and
`r fmt(abs(pct(sp[["log2(dheas)"]]$ratio)), 1)`% lower for each doubling of DHEA-S, and differs by race/ethnicity and
menopausal status. With the covariates of the initial model, each additional kilogram of skeletal muscle mass was
associated with `r fmt(abs(pct(R$shbg_outcome$submitted_smm$ratio)), 1)`% lower SHBG. The primary analysis keeps
skeletal muscle mass as the dependent variable because that is how the question is posed in the literature; the design
is cross-sectional and neither model identifies a direction of effect.
